summary: This informational RFC discusses the sanctions that could be applied to violators of IETF intellectual property rights policy, who applies them and how, to reduce ambiguity.

eli5.summary: If someone breaks the rules about who owns an idea, this explains the possible consequences and who decides.

questions: what happens if someone violates ietf ipr policy
what sanctions exist for ipr disclosure violations
what is a posting rights action
who applies ipr sanctions in the ietf
subtitle: The menu of penalties the IETF can apply to people who break its patent disclosure rules, and who chooses them.

tldr.problem: The IETF takes its intellectual property disclosure policy seriously, but it was ambiguous what sanctions apply to violators and who applies them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6701 lists ten available sanctions in rough order of severity, names working group chairs and area directors as the usual first actors, and gives guidance on fairness and on choosing a sanction.
tldr.outcome: It adds no new powers: all the sanctions already exist in IETF processes, and any of them can be appealed.

facts.label: Posting Rights Action duration
facts.value: A year, unless revoked or extended

today: RFC 6701 is an Informational RFC and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The sanctions it lists are described as already available in IETF processes.

sections.title: The Policy Being Protected
sections.content:
The IETF's IPR policy is set out in RFC 3979 (RFC 3979, BCP 79), and this document only summarizes it. Each participant is responsible for disclosing, or ensuring disclosure of, Intellectual Property Rights when they are aware of the IPR, it is relevant to the IETF work they are participating in, and it is owned by them or by a company that employs or sponsors their work.

Timeliness matters but is not precisely defined. A disclosure on a published RFC is likely to be far more disruptive than one on an early individual draft. A participant who cannot disclose in time can instead refrain from contributing to that technology. Third parties may also disclose, with reasons.

The sanctions here are administrative ones imposed through IETF processes. They do not limit any legal remedies available outside the IETF. A companion document, RFC 6702, covers promoting compliance.
sections.eli5: If you know about a patent that touches the group's work, you must say so in good time. If you will not say, you should stay out of that work.

sections.title: Who Starts and Decides
sections.content:
Any participant can draw attention to an apparent violation by emailing a short summary of the facts to the appropriate IETF mailing list. Normally the working group chairs act first when a working group is involved, and area directors act first in other cases. The first step is usually to gather facts and talk with the people involved.

Chairs choose the action because they are closest to the details. Where there is no working group, or the decision is uncomfortable for the chairs, the responsible area director can guide or direct it.

The document separates sanctions from how a working group handles a disclosure. Reworking a draft to avoid disclosed IPR is not itself a sanction, though the disruption of a late disclosure can be a reason to sanction the individuals.
sections.eli5: Anyone can raise a flag. The adults in charge of the group, the chairs, usually look into it first and decide what to do.

sections.title: The Available Sanctions
sections.content:
Section 4 lists ten sanctions, labeled a to j, in approximate order of severity. The list is not exhaustive, more than one can be used, and the order is not a rule. They run from a private discussion, through formal private or public warnings and naming the failure to the working group, to refusing or removing the person as document editor, moving their name from the authors list to the Acknowledgements, deprecating or rejecting a document, and posting restrictions.

A temporary suspension of posting rights on a specific list can be applied by working group chairs for no more than 30 days. The heaviest is a Posting Rights Action under RFC 3683, which removes posting rights on a particular IETF mailing list for a year unless revoked or extended, and which an area director introduces for consideration by the IETF community and the IESG.

Authors who supplied text have a right to be recognized, so a name cannot be removed entirely unless their text is removed too.
sections.eli5: The list starts with a quiet chat and ends with being muted on the group's mailing lists for a year. Contributors still get credit for what they wrote.

sections.title: Fairness, Appeals and Choosing a Sanction
sections.content:
Anyone who feels unfairly treated, or thinks a decision was wrong, may appeal using the procedures in Section 6.5 of RFC 2026. Any of the sanctions can be appealed this way.

The person applying a sanction should match its severity to the offense and apply judgment equitably over time, and should seek opinions from colleagues or the community when in doubt. Appendix A offers non-exhaustive, unweighted questions: how long the person has been active, how late the disclosure is, whether they are a major or minor contributor, whether they have a reason for forgetting the IPR, how speedy and humble their apology was, and how disruptive the disclosure is.
sections.eli5: Anyone punished can ask for a second look. The people deciding should think about the whole story, such as how late the news came and whether it was an honest slip.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Nothing in the document directly affects the operational security of the Internet. It does argue that ignoring the IPR policy can be disruptive to standards development and so may be regarded as an attack on the IETF's correct operation. A late disclosure, or none at all, could even represent an attack on the use of deployed equipment.
sections.eli5: Hiding a patent until late can mess up the group's work and the equipment people already use, so the group treats it as a serious problem.
